title: What's your setup?
author: pietrzm
selftext:
Hey!

How your day-to-day setup looks like with AI?

What tools are you using and where do run your agent sessions? Are you using existing engines or rolling your own? 

And how the hell you iterate on assets created by AI without constant digging through the files and loading it manually for preview?

I've read so much on people AI setups and I think it's super interesting thing to share or even boast about it.

comments.author: pietrzm
comments.body: I'll start that I heavily rely on CI pipelines, but I'm mostly a dev, just starting gamedev with AI. I'm still trying to figure out best ergonomics for asset creation and worthwhile process

replies.author: throwaway09234023322
replies.body: If you figure out asset creation, let me know. Lol. Right now, sol seems to do a much better job with it because it can generate images itself and then use the blender mcp for the 3d assets. Claude seems to waste a lot of time with the mcp and can't do much as far as image gen. Just my experience. I haven't tried other asset gen services like tripo

comments.author: BHave_TRO
comments.body:
Hi,   
for [https://storegga.org](https://storegga.org) I use:

\-- Meshy, for Image to 3D Conversion  
\-- NanoBanana for Keyart  
\-- Qwen 3.8 local vor Development  
\-- Claude Opus 5.5 to instruct Qwen  
\-- UE 5.8 with MCP  
\-- Blender with MCP  
\-- 3 machines. 2 Laptops (RTX4070, i9, 32MB RAM and T1000, i7, 64MB RAM) and one Server (2x3090) Threadripper 3xxx, 96MB Ram  
\-- Python DSP Scripts for SoundFX  
\-- Google labs Flow Music for the Theme  
\-- VoiceStudio for different voices

I'm reviewing the Assets and make my adjustments. Sometimes manually sometimes I trigger the AI to do it all over with another more specific prompt.

If you have any questions about it, feel free to ask,

comments.author: Careless_Road8873
comments.body:
Mine's pretty boring on the tool side, which I think is why it works.

Engine is Godot 4. I didn't want the AI building an engine on top of building a game. Claude writes almost all of the code. It runs in its own cloud workspace with a copy of the project and copies the changed files into my project folder when it's done. I open Godot, play, and tell it what's wrong. Exporting and uploading to itch are two .bat files it wrote, so shipping a build is a couple of double clicks.

Images come from ChatGPT, with the same style block pasted at the start of every chat and one reference picture attached to every prompt. Animations start as Veo clips, and a script cuts them into frames, lines them up and packs them for the engine.

For your last question, the thing that saved me was making the game take its own screenshots. There's a small test scene for almost every screen that loads it, renders it and saves a PNG. Claude runs those and looks at the pictures before I do, and when it changes art it sends me a before and after side by side. I only go into the files when something looks wrong in a picture.

Two other things I wouldn't skip. A long handover file in the project that every new session reads first, so decisions don't get forgotten. And about 470 tests that run on every change, because the AI breaks old stuff quietly when nothing is checking.

replies.author: pietrzm
replies.body:
I've learned that you can generate ChatGPT Images directly in Codex CLI. I definitely can recommend that as you can tell Claude to use it as a tool lol

The screenshot bit is interesting

replies.author: Careless_Road8873
replies.body:
Good tip, I'll look into it. I've kept the image side manual so far on purpose though. Picking and throwing out pictures is the one part I don't want to hand over, it's most of what makes the game look like one game.

The screenshot setup is simpler than it sounds. Godot can run a scene from the command line, so each test scene opens the game, jumps straight to one window (the market, a fight, the character sheet) with made-up data, waits a few frames and saves the viewport as a PNG. It runs on a virtual display so nothing pops up. Then Claude just opens the image like any other file. Most of the bugs I'd have found by playing show up there first, like text running off a panel or a figure standing on the wrong spot.

comments.author: Turbulent-Upstairs47
comments.body: For the asset preview problem, I'd put candidates in a little test scene with the actual game camera and lighting. A model can look great in a viewer and be unreadable at gameplay distance. Keep the old version beside the new one, too. Much easier to judge whether “better” is actually better.
